transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-02
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Atlas - ML Eng), Priya Nair (Atlas - Platform Lead), Sam Torres (Atlas - CTO)

Summary: weekly POC sync focused on benchmark recap vs baseline provider (BaselineCloud). Reviewed p50/p95/p99 latencies, sustained throughput, warm vs cold cache behavior, and tuning knobs (batch size, quantization, KV caching). Agreed on next steps to share detailed traces and run a live traffic throughput pass.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check, can you all hear me?
[00:03] Jordan Lee: Yeah loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:08] Maya Chen: Cool, so agenda for today — recap the benchmark numbers we ran last week, compare to the baseline provider you mentioned (BaselineCloud), go over the tuning tweaks Liam recommended, and agree next steps.
[00:22] Priya Nair: That works, main thing for us is p99 tail and sustained throughput during peak ingestion windows.
[00:28] Liam Patel: yep, we'll focus on those. Quick note about the testbed: Redwood ran on an A100-similar instance with q4f16 quantization and our KV caching warmed; baseline runs we received from Atlas were on a mix of GPU types, looks like BaselineCloud used T4-backed instances for the small model tests — that will affect tail latency.
[00:47] Sam Torres: just to confirm, the model is the open-llm-XL v1 variant?
[00:52] Jordan Lee: it's the finetuned open-llm-xl-v1-512 context, yes. Prompts averaged ~120 tokens, response sizes ~80 tokens.
[00:59] Liam Patel: ok cool. So headline numbers: p50 we measured ~42ms per token equivalent (end-to-end inference p50 ~120ms for the full response), p95 ~280ms, and p99 ~460ms in our baseline-balanced run with warm KV. BaselineCloud numbers you sent show p50 ~65ms and p99 ~920ms for similar prompt/response sizes.
[01:17] Jordan Lee: those p99s on BaselineCloud look right from our logs, the tail is nasty. I guess their instances spin up slower?
[01:23] Maya Chen: there are a couple things that drive that — hardware (T4 vs A100), kernel selection, and how KV cache/warmth is managed. We observed that when the KV cache is warm, our p99 drops significantly to ~180ms for identical requests (we ran a warm-only sweep).
[01:40] Priya Nair: can you repeat that? you said p99 drops to 180ms when warm?
[01:43] Liam Patel: yeah so we did two passes: a cold-start-like pass (cache cold, initial requests) and a warm-pass (after steady-state traffic). Cold p99 was ~460ms; warm steady-state p99 was ~180ms. BaselineCloud didn't have the same warm caching behavior in their setup, so their warm vs cold delta was smaller but higher overall tail.
[02:02] Jordan Lee: that aligns with our day-of-week spikes — after idle periods the tail balloons.
[02:07] Sam Torres: throughput numbers — how do you compare? tokens/sec etc.
[02:11] Liam Patel: for throughput, on the same instance class we pushed batch sizes up gradually. At batch size 8 with q4f16 we got ~720 tokens/sec sustained. BaselineCloud on their T4-style instances peaked around ~310 tokens/sec before token-level backpressure started adding latency.
[02:30] Jordan Lee: that's a pretty big diff. Are you normalizing for sequence length?
[02:34] Liam Patel: yep, tests used the same prompt and response distribution; median prompt len 120, median response len 80, we report tokens/sec aggregated over 60s windows.
[02:42] Priya Nair: any notes on cost? BaselineCloud is quoting lower cost but their perf is worse — we care about cost per successful inference within SLO as you said.
[02:51] Maya Chen: right — typical naive cost-per-token can be lower for the cheapest instances but if you factor in retries, tail latency penalties, and operational overhead (more instances to hit throughput), Redwood's cost per successful-inference-at-SLO is materially lower in our models. We'll include a cost per 1M effective tokens sheet in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[03:08] Jordan Lee: can you quantify "materially lower"?
[03:11] Maya Chen: from our modeling on your workload, BaselineCloud's effective cost per 1M tokens at p95 SLO would be about 1.6x the Redwood estimate, mostly due to needing more parallel instances to compensate for lower throughput and higher tails. We'll include the calc.
[03:26] Liam Patel: a couple technical notes on the tuning we discussed: 1) batching: moving from batch=1 to batch=4 decreased p50 slightly but increased throughput significantly; 2) quantization: q4f16 gave us very close quality with about 1.8x throughput versus fp16; 3) kernel tuning: using our sequence-optimized kernels reduces KV-copy overhead on long contexts.
[03:47] Priya Nair: what's the impact on quality with q4f16? Our compliance folks worry about hallucination changes when we change quant.
[03:54] Liam Patel: good question — perceptual quality was essentially unchanged on our eval set. We ran BLEU/ROUGE-ish checks and spot human eval on the finetuned model; differences were negligible for your prompt set. For safety-critical prompts we can keep fp16 if you prefer, cost goes up but tail improves or stays similar depending on instance.
[04:11] Jordan Lee: are any model changes needed to hit p99 targets?
[04:14] Liam Patel: no architecture changes required. This is mostly serving-level optimizations: quant, batch size, and keeping the KV cache warm using a short-lived keep-alive traffic pattern or pre-warming strategy before expected traffic windows.
[04:25] Sam Torres: pre-warming — how heavy of a footprint is that operationally?
[04:28] Liam Patel: you can do lightweight pre-warm with synthetic low-cost requests that only prime the KV; the token cost is minimal relative to reruns on tail failures. We can provide a small tool to orchestrate it.
[04:36] Jordan Lee: can you walk through the p99 timeline detail? Like a trace so we can see where time is spent.
[04:40] Liam Patel: yes, we'll surface a per-request timeline: queue wait, model forward, KV lookup, kernel overhead. For our p99 traces the long tail is mostly queue+kernel stalls during cold tails on smaller hardware. On Redwood's tuned setup kernel stalls were greatly reduced.
[04:55] Maya Chen: I'll add that trace export to the spreadsheet share. Liam, do you have any notes on the fallback behavior if we hit saturation?
[05:01] Liam Patel: yes — Redwood can be configured to fall back to a smaller model variant or route to dedicated capacity if latency crosses threshold; we can do gradual degradation so you preserve utility while protecting SLOs. BaselineCloud offered a single scaling policy which was more binary and caused some request loss during bursts.
[05:18] Priya Nair: security question — you mentioned KMS and audit logs earlier; can you re-state what you can provide for private runs?
[05:23] Maya Chen: for Private we support customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations can be discussed in detail, and we stream audit logs to your SIEM via secure forwarders. I'll attach SOC2 documentation and a network diagram.
[05:33] Jordan Lee: please include the VPC peering steps and firewall rules. Our infra team will need that.
[05:37] Maya Chen: yes will include.
[05:39] Sam Torres: any anomalies in the run we should be worried about?
[05:42] Liam Patel: one anomaly — one of the baseline-comparison runs we received had a misconfigured autoscaler which reduced concurrency mid-test; we flagged that and re-ran, but that explains one of the outlier spikes in their initial CSV. We included both raw and corrected runs in the sheet.
[05:58] Jordan Lee: thanks for cleaning that up.
[06:00] Maya Chen: ok before we wrap, quick recap and next steps — Liam will export per-model p99 traces and KV hit-rate splits, I'll send the benchmark spreadsheet + cost modeling + SOC2/network docs, Jordan will run the live throughput pass and share logs. We'll schedule the infra deep-dive for next week. Anything else?
[06:18] Priya Nair: can you also add an example of the keep-alive script and expected token cost for a 1 hour pre-warm window?
[06:25] Liam Patel: yes, will add example and cost calc.
[06:27] Jordan Lee: great. Thanks everyone.
[06:29] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
[06:32] -- End of meeting --

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcription had a few mis-heard items ("K-V cash" instead of "KV cache", "Redwood Dedicate" occasionally). Speakers sometimes overlap; labels are accurate most of the time but there are a few speaker attribution quirks in the raw export.

References shared during call: 
- Benchmark spreadsheet link (shared in chat): https://redwood-internal/benchmarks/atlas-poc-2025-04-02 (note: link placeholder)
- SOC2 + network diagram (sent post-meeting)
- Keep-alive pre-warm script (snippet attached)

Recap (short): Redwood shows materially lower tail latency and higher sustained throughput vs the BaselineCloud runs provided, particularly after KV cache warm. Action items assigned and next steps scheduled for sharing traces and running a live throughput pass.
